name: CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide)

b.x: Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide, or CGRP (alpha isoform, encoded by the CALCA gene; CAS 83652-28-2), is a 37-amino-acid neuropeptide and one of the most potent microvascular vasodilators identified to date ([PMID 23162536](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23162536/)). Reviews put it 10 to 1,000 times more potent than acetylcholine at widening small blood vessels ([PMID 25287861](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25287861/), [PMID 23162536](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23162536/)). Four FDA-approved monoclonal antibodies and three gepant receptor blockers exist because of this single molecule. The path from peptide to drug target started with two findings. Goadsby and colleagues [1] measured raised CGRP in jugular venous blood during spontaneous migraine attacks. Then Lassen's group [2] showed in 2002 that a 20-minute IV CGRP infusion gave all nine analyzed migraine patients a headache. Three had migraine-like attacks. That provocation model became the foundation for developing erenumab (Aimovig), fremanezumab (Ajovy), galcanezumab (Emgality), eptinezumab (Vyepti), ubrogepant (Ubrelvy), rimegepant (Nurtec), and atogepant (Qulipta), all approved between 2018 and 2022. Beyond migraine, CGRP shows cardioprotective properties in ischemia-reperfusion models and accelerates wound closure in diabetic mouse models (Lu YZ et al., Nature 2024) [3]. But the peptide itself has no approved therapeutic indication. That 6.9-minute plasma half-life requires continuous IV infusion, and the potent systemic vasodilation makes outpatient use impractical. CGRP remains a research tool, not a therapeutic product.

CGRP binds a heterodimeric receptor built from calcitonin receptor-like receptor (CLR) and receptor activity-modifying protein 1 (RAMP1). A third protein, receptor component protein (RCP), locks in the G protein coupling. Once CGRP docks onto CLR/RAMP1, the primary cascade runs through Gs signaling. Adenylyl cyclase fires up, intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) rises, and protein kinase A (PKA) gets to work. In vascular smooth muscle, PKA phosphorylates KATP channels and myosin light chain phosphatase. Both actions relax the muscle wall and dilate the vessel. Some vascular beds add an endothelium-dependent layer; CGRP activates endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS), releasing nitric oxide for additional vasodilation. The receptor also signals through beta-arrestin pathways after internalization into endosomes. Sustained cAMP production continues inside the cell even after plasma CGRP is gone. That endosomal signaling likely explains why vasodilatory effects persist 20 to 40 minutes beyond the peptide's 6.9-minute clearance. In trigeminal sensory neurons, CGRP released from peripheral terminals in the dura triggers a cascade: dural vasodilation, mast cell degranulation, plasma protein extravasation, and sensitization of second-order trigeminocervical neurons. This is the core pathophysiology of migraine. CGRP also sensitizes its own release from neighboring neurons, creating a positive feedback loop that sustains and amplifies the attack.
CGRP benefits center on vasodilation, cardioprotection, and neurovascular biology.

Between 10 and 1,000 times more potent than acetylcholine at widening small blood vessels, depending on the review (Russell 2014, [PMID 25287861](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25287861/); Kokkoris 2012, [PMID 23162536](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23162536/)). Both rank it among the most potent vasodilators known.
Reduces infarct size in ischemia-reperfusion injury models through PKC-epsilon and KATP channel-dependent ischemic preconditioning pathways.
An engineered eCGRP construct accelerated wound closure roughly 2.5x in diabetic mouse models (Lu YZ et al., Nature 2024) [3], driven by keratinocyte proliferation and microvascular perfusion.
Gastroprotective: maintains mucosal blood flow and suppresses gastric acid secretion in the GI tract.
Anti-hypertensive properties confirmed in preclinical models of both pulmonary and systemic hypertension.
Neuroprotective effects shown in stroke and traumatic brain injury animal models, with reduced infarct volume and improved functional recovery scores.

CGRP is one of the most potent microvascular vasodilators identified ([PMID 23162536](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23162536/)) and the central molecular target in migraine pathophysiology.

Dosing studied: IV infusion for 20 minutes. The migraine provocation standard is 1.5 mcg/min, 30 mcg total (PMID 37815254); Lassen 2002 used 2 mcg/min (PMID 11993614). Kraenzlin 1985 gave synthetic rat CGRP at about 0.09 to 0.7 mcg/min for a 70 kg adult (PMID 3922013). The 3 mcg/min (60 mcg) top of the tier range is unsourced. SC route: no established dose (unsourced).

Exogenous CGRP infusion is validated as the gold-standard migraine provocation model. Cardioprotective and wound-healing effects are documented in preclinical models; no approved human therapeutic indication exists for the peptide itself.
Key Study

Lassen LH et al. (Cephalalgia 2002, PMID 11993614): a 20-minute IV CGRP infusion caused headache in all 9 analyzed migraineurs and migraine-like attacks in 3. Goadsby PJ et al. (1990, PMID 2454066): serum CGRP elevated in jugular blood during spontaneous migraine attacks. Lu YZ et al. (Nature 2024, PMID 38538784): engineered eCGRP construct accelerated wound closure ~2.5x in diabetic mouse models.
Limitations

6.9-minute half-life requires continuous IV infusion; no human therapeutic trials for cardioprotection or wound healing have completed Phase II. 2024 wound healing data (PMID 38538784) used an ECM-anchored eCGRP construct, not native peptide. No full-length agonist CGRP with extended half-life has reached clinical trials as of October 2026 (ClinicalTrials.gov).

b.x: CGRP is not a self-administration peptide. This needs to be stated plainly because the peptide shows up in search results alongside injectable peptides that people do use at home. The 6.9-minute half-life means subcutaneous injection produces a brief, unpredictable hemodynamic event with no sustained benefit. Every published human study used IV infusion with continuous blood pressure monitoring. Infusion prep is a job for the research pharmacy, not a home step. The migraine provocation standard is 1.5 mcg/min for 20 minutes, 30 mcg in total. That dose is diluted into normal saline and run through an infusion pump, so there is no syringe draw to work out. The detail most people miss: CGRP adsorbs to glass and plastic surfaces at low concentrations. Below 10 mcg/mL, add 0.1% BSA (bovine serum albumin) as a carrier protein and use siliconized or protein low-bind containers. Skip this step and your actual delivered dose could be noticeably lower than intended.
Cycling Protocol

No established human cycling protocol exists for exogenous CGRP administration. The extremely short half-life (~6.9 minutes) necessitates continuous IV infusion for sustained effects, which is impractical outside controlled research settings. Human infusion studies have typically used single-dose protocols (1.5 to 2 mcg/min for 20 minutes). Repeated dosing may lead to tachyphylaxis of vasodilatory responses. Cycling parameters shown are theoretical placeholders. Any investigational use requires continuous hemodynamic monitoring.
CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide) Continuous

No established cycling protocol exists for exogenous CGRP. Human research has been limited exclusively to single-dose IV infusion sessions due to extreme hemodynamic risk. Receptor desensitization via rapid CLR/RAMP1 internalization occurs within minutes of exposure. Tachyphylaxis of the vasodilatory response is documented with repeat infusions in the same session. The cyclingProtocol values in the source file (onWeeks: 1, offWeeks: 4) are explicitly acknowledged placeholders with no scientific basis: any investigational repeat use requires full hemodynamic recovery between sessions.
Attenuated vasodilatory response on repeat infusion within the same session (receptor internalization)
Tachycardia persisting >30 min post-infusion (insufficient washout before next dose)
Blood pressure failing to return within 10 mmHg of baseline before next infusion
Migraine headache onset during or immediately following infusion (abort and reassess protocol)

Confirm setting: continuous blood pressure monitoring (intra-arterial line preferred), ECG telemetry, peripheral IV access, and vasopressor (phenylephrine 50 to 100 mcg IV) on standby. Subject supine.

Pharmacy prep: the research pharmacy dissolves the lyophilized peptide and dilutes the session dose into normal saline for the infusion pump. Gently swirl until dissolved. Do not vortex. Nothing is drawn into a syringe for injection.
Set the pump: the standard 1.5 mcg/min rate gives 30 mcg over 20 minutes. Use protein low-bind tubing; add 0.1% BSA to the diluent if the concentration falls below 10 mcg/mL.
Begin infusion at target rate Record baseline blood pressure and heart rate immediately before starting.

Monitor continuously: BP and HR every 1 to 2 minutes during infusion. Alert thresholds are systolic drop greater than 20 mmHg from baseline, absolute systolic below 90 mmHg, or sustained HR above 130 bpm.
Stop infusion immediately if: systolic BP drops more than 30 mmHg, HR exceeds 130 sustained, SpO2 falls below 92%, or subject requests discontinuation.

Post-infusion monitoring: keep subject supine for 60 minutes minimum. Record headache severity (VAS or NRS) at 30 min, 1h, 2h, 4h, and 12h. Do not allow standing until BP returns within 10 mmHg of baseline.
Storage: reconstituted solution is stable for up to 48 hours at 2 to 8 degrees C. Do not refreeze. Prepare fresh on study day when possible.
Alternative Routes
Intravenous infusion (standard research route)
Cited infusions ran 1.5 to 2 mcg/min for 20 minutes, 30 to 40 mcg total (PMID 37815254, 11993614); the 60 mcg tier (3 mcg/min) is unsourced. Reference route (100% bioavailability).
Infusion pump required. Peripheral IV line adequate; central line preferred for high-dose protocols. Continuous hemodynamic monitoring mandatory.
Subcutaneous injection (investigational)
Unsourced: no SC dose has been established. The 10 to 60 mcg figures are the IV infusion totals, not a tested SC dose. No established SC protocol in modern literature.
Local erythema and warmth at injection site expected (local vasodilatory effect). Hemodynamic monitoring still required. Not used in contemporary migraine or cardioprotection research protocols.

Generic / Research
Research-grade alpha-CGRP: ~$200–$450 per 1 mg lyophilized vial (lab-reagent pricing). Custom bulk synthesis: ~$80–$180/mg at scale. No gray-market consumer supply identified.

Profound, dose-dependent hypotension is the most serious risk with exogenous CGRP. IV infusion studies report systolic blood pressure drops of 10 to 30 mmHg. At high doses, blood pressure can fall far enough to require IV fluid bolus or vasopressor intervention with phenylephrine (50 to 100 mcg IV). This is not a mild inconvenience; it's a medical event that demands continuous hemodynamic monitoring and vasopressor standby before any infusion begins. Facial flushing occurs in virtually all subjects at pharmacological doses. Published figures put it at approximately 99%. The flushing reflects CGRP's vasodilatory mechanism acting on cutaneous vasculature. Warmth, cutaneous erythema, and a sensation of heat throughout the body accompany the flushing. Reflex tachycardia follows the blood pressure drop. Heart rate increases as the cardiovascular system compensates for reduced vascular resistance. A 2026 FAERS analysis [5] flagged palpitation signals across the entire CGRP pathway drug class, raising the monitoring bar even further. The migraine provocation effect is perhaps the most distinctive side effect of any peptide. In migraine-susceptible individuals, CGRP infusion triggers delayed migraine-like attacks. In the 2023 REFORM study, 110 of 139 people with migraine (79%) had one within 12 hours of a 20-minute infusion [6]. This reflects sustained trigeminal sensitization rather than ongoing peripheral CGRP activity, since the peptide clears in under 7 minutes. Nausea, dizziness, and lightheadedness related to blood pressure reduction are common during and immediately after infusion. Long-term effects of exogenous CGRP are unknown. All published human data comes from single infusions or very short courses. Theoretical concerns include exacerbation of inflammatory conditions (CGRP drives neurogenic inflammation) and interference with bone metabolism. Contraindications are strict. Hypotension or hemodynamic instability, active migraine, severe cardiovascular disease, concurrent potent antihypertensives, pregnancy, and breastfeeding all disqualify a subject. Administration outside a setting with continuous hemodynamic monitoring, IV access, and vasopressor availability is not appropriate for any reason.
Common Issues & Solutions

Hypotension (>20 mmHg systolic drop): Have IV fluid bolus (250–500 mL saline) and vasopressor (phenylephrine 50–100 mcg IV) ready before infusion starts. Keep subject supine during infusion and 30–60 min after. Do not allow standing until BP returns to within 10 mmHg of baseline.

Surface adsorption at low concentrations: CGRP adsorbs strongly to glass and polypropylene at concentrations below ~10 mcg/mL. Add 0.1% BSA as carrier protein to diluent and use siliconized or protein low-bind containers for accurate dosing at research concentrations.

Delayed migraine headache (1–5h post-infusion): Pre-screen subjects for migraine history if provocation is not the study endpoint. If headache develops, sumatriptan 50–100 mg oral or 6 mg SC is effective and validates the CGRP mechanism of the headache.

Solution instability: Reconstituted CGRP is highly labile. Use within 48 hours at 2–8°C. Do not freeze reconstituted solution; multiple freeze-thaw cycles abolish activity. Prepare fresh on the study day when possible.

Tachyphylaxis on repeat infusion: Vasodilatory response can diminish with repeated CGRP infusions in the same session (CLR/RAMP1 internalization). Allow ≥30 min between infusions and confirm baseline hemodynamic recovery before re-dosing.

b.x: Source: Plasma t1/2 of immunoreactive CGRP is approximately 6.9 minutes (the fast phase of a two-phase decay) in humans given synthetic rat CGRP by IV infusion (Kraenzlin et al., 1985, PMID 3922013). No single clearance route is established; mast cell tryptase and matrix metalloproteinase-2 both cleave CGRP (Kokkoris et al., 2012, PMID 23162536)

CGRP peptide has no FDA-approved therapeutic indication. Its regulatory status is research-only. The peptide is sold only as a lab reagent for laboratory and clinical research use. Seven drugs targeting the CGRP pathway are FDA-approved for migraine (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab, ubrogepant, rimegepant, atogepant), but these block CGRP signaling rather than providing it. The peptide itself is a different product entirely. No consumer gray-market supply chain exists for CGRP. WADA status is not applicable as there is no performance-improving use case. Any human administration requires IRB approval, informed consent, and a clinical research protocol with appropriate hemodynamic safety measures. This content is for educational and research reference purposes only. It does not constitute medical advice, and nothing here should be interpreted as a recommendation to administer CGRP to humans outside of approved research protocols.
Evidence grade: Small human studies only (Peptide Evidence Gap, October 2026)

faqs.q: If CGRP causes migraines, why are anti-CGRP drugs the treatment?
faqs.a: During a migraine attack, trigeminal sensory neurons release excessive CGRP, causing dural vasodilation and central sensitization. Anti-CGRP antibodies block this excess from acting at its receptor. Exogenous CGRP infusion mimics the excess seen during attacks; it doesn't treat migraine, it provokes it. The drugs target pathologically elevated CGRP, not the peptide's normal physiological role.

Alpha-CGRP (37 AA, encoded by CALCA via alternative splicing of calcitonin mRNA) predominates in sensory and central nervous system neurons; this is the isoform relevant to migraine and vascular physiology. Beta-CGRP (37 AA, 94% sequence homology, encoded by CALCB) is primarily expressed in enteric neurons.

faqs.q: Are anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies a cardiovascular risk?
faqs.a: Emerging signal. A 2024 Neurology study found a modestly increased composite cardiovascular risk with CGRP inhibitor initiation. CGRP is cardioprotective, so blocking it long-term could theoretically reduce ischemic protection. Short-term clinical trial data (25,000+ patient-years) has not shown MACE increase, but this remains under active surveillance.

faqs.q: Why isn't CGRP developed as a drug for heart disease or wound healing?
faqs.a: The 6.9-minute half-life requires continuous IV infusion, impractical for chronic use. Potent systemic vasodilation limits dosing and causes hypotension. And the anti-CGRP drug class arrived and captured commercial interest in the pathway before agonist development could compete.

faqs.q: Could exogenous CGRP have therapeutic applications despite its short half-life?
faqs.a: Active investigation. The cardioprotective application (ischemia-reperfusion injury) may be compatible with a single-dose or brief infusion protocol. Modified CGRP analogs with longer half-lives are in preclinical development but none have reached clinical trials as of 2026.

summary: Between 10 and 1,000 times more potent than acetylcholine at relaxing small blood vessels, depending on the review. CGRP (Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide) is a 37-amino-acid neuropeptide that became the molecular foundation for the most successful migraine drug class developed in the past two decades. Four monoclonal antibodies and three small-molecule gepants now target this single peptide pathway. The peptide itself, however, remains a research-only compound. A plasma half-life of 6.9 minutes and potent hypotensive effects have kept exogenous CGRP confined to controlled IV infusion studies. Researchers use it to probe trigeminal neurovascular physiology, cardiovascular regulation, and wound healing biology.
